To use the past infinitive after dopo: dopo aver visto, dopo essere arrivati.
To use prima di, senza, pur di + infinitive (same subject).
To use the present gerund with a causal or temporal meaning: essendo stanca, guardando il quadro.
To use the past gerund for a previous action: avendo finito, essendo arrivati.
To use the absolute participle: arrivati a Malta, visto il quadro, finita la visita.
To know when you CAN'T use the implicit form (when the subject changes).
Valletta, February. Dr Camilleri leads Giulia and Matei into the oratory of St John's Co-Cathedral. The light is dim. On the far wall, enormous, hangs the "Beheading of Saint John the Baptist".
Here we are. Before turning on the lights, I wanted you to see it like this, in the half-light. As the knights saw it.
It's enormous. I didn't think… Having seen it only in books, I didn't imagine it was so big.
More than five metres. Caravaggio painted it in 1608, after arriving here as a fugitive.
The same year as Totò. Once he'd finished this, he fled to Sicily and painted Saint Lucy.
Exactly. And look here, at the bottom, in the saint's blood. The signature.
"F. Michelang.o." He wrote it using the blood. Without even changing brush.
Looking at it closely, you can see some tiny cracks. That's why we need you, Dr Esposito.
Giulia? Are you all right? You haven't said a word for five minutes.
I'm fine. It's just that… just to work on this painting, I think I'd walk here.
That won't be necessary. Given your enthusiasm, I'll send you the contract on Monday.
Wait, doctor. Before signing, we need to see something important.
"visto il suo entusiasmo" = given your enthusiasm
A Maltese word: J is read as I (Y). gal-la-REE-ya.
An explicit clause has a conjugated verb (dopo che abbiamo visto). An implicit one has an infinitive, gerund or participle (dopo aver visto). The implicit form is shorter and more elegant:
Dopo che abbiamo visto il quadro, abbiamo deciso.
Dopo aver visto il quadro, abbiamo deciso.
Prima che partissimo, abbiamo salutato la nonna.
Prima di partire, abbiamo salutato la nonna.
Quando siamo arrivati a Malta, siamo andati alla cattedrale.
Arrivati a Malta, siamo andati alla cattedrale.
The implicit form is usually possible only when the subject is THE SAME in both clauses.
2. The infinitive: dopo, prima di, senza, pur di
Dopo aver visto il quadro… / Dopo essere arrivati…
È rimasta lì senza dire una parola.
Pur di lavorarci, andrei a piedi.
Invece di dormire, guardava il mare.
The past infinitive = avere / essere + participle: aver visto, essere arrivato/a/i/e. With essere the participle agrees: dopo essere arrivate, le ragazze…
Essendo stanca, Viola si è addormentata.
Guardandola da vicino, si vedono delle crepe.
Avendo finito il lavoro, siamo usciti.
Essendo arrivati tardi, non abbiamo cenato.
Pronouns attach to the gerund: guardandola, avendolo visto, essendosene andato.
The past participle alone, at the start of the sentence, expresses an action completed beforehand. You saw it in chapter 40; now you use it with more confidence:
Visto il quadro, Giulia non ha avuto più dubbi.
Dopo che ha visto il quadro…
Finita la visita, siamo andati al porto.
Visto il suo entusiasmo, le mando il contratto.
Dato che ho visto il suo entusiasmo…
The participle agrees with the noun after it (finita la visita, visti i quadri) or with the subject, for verbs with essere (arrivati a Malta).
5. When you CAN'T use the implicit form
Prima di partire Giulia, Matei ha chiamato.
Prima che Giulia partisse, Matei ha chiamato.
"Prima di" + infinitive (same subject), but "prima che" + congiuntivo (different subject). You saw this in chapter 54.
After arriving, we went to the cathedral.
Just to work on this painting, I'd walk.
Prima Giulia partire, Matei ha chiamato.
"Instead of sleeping, he was looking at the sea":
Invece che dorma, guardava il mare.

They left one Friday morning in February, from Pisa, on a flight that took an hour and a half. Before leaving the house, Giulia had checked the passports three times, Matei had packed a bag full of toys for Viola, and Graziella had secretly slipped into the suitcase a glass jar full of ribollita, wrapped in four layers of newspaper. "You never know," she had said, when Matei found it at the airport, at baggage control. The jar was confiscated. Graziella, told on the phone, said that Malta was getting off to a bad start.

Having woken up at five, Viola fell asleep on the plane even before take-off, with her cloth bunny under her arm. She woke up only during landing, when the island appeared in the window: small, golden, surrounded by a sea so blue it looked fake. Viola stared at it for a long time, open-mouthed. Then she said her first Maltese word, which was actually Italian, but which she pronounced with great solemnity: "Sea-ino."

Once at the airport, they found Dr Camilleri himself waiting for them, a sixty-year-old man with white hair, round glasses and perfect Italian, learned, he explained, by watching Italian television as a child. "In Malta we all did," he said, laughing. "Before learning English at school, we already knew the Sanremo songs by heart." Having loaded the luggage into the car, he drove them towards Valletta along a winding road between honey-coloured stone walls.

Valletta won them over in ten minutes. It was a small city built on a peninsula, with straight streets running down to the sea on both sides, like the lines of an exercise book. On the house fronts were enclosed balconies of painted wood, green, red, blue, which Camilleri called "gallarija". From the bastions you could see the Grand Harbour, the enormous port, with the fishermen's colourful boats and the ferries to Sicily. "From here, in 1608, Caravaggio looked towards Italy," said Camilleri. "Thinking, probably, that he would never go back."

Having left their suitcases at the hotel, they went straight to the Co-Cathedral. From the outside it looked like a fortress: a plain, almost severe façade with two bell towers. But as soon as she crossed the threshold, Giulia stopped and held her breath. Inside, everything was gold. The walls, the vaults, the columns were covered in gilded decoration, and the floor was made of four hundred tombstones of coloured marble, one for each knight buried beneath, with coats of arms, skeletons, angels and Latin inscriptions. Viola, as soon as she was inside, started running over the tombstones shouting "Figo!" until Matei picked her up.

Having crossed the nave, Camilleri led them into a side chapel, the oratory, where the light was much dimmer. He stopped in front of a wooden door and turned to them. "Before going in," he said, "I ask you one thing. Don't look at the painting straight away. Look first at the floor, then at the walls, then raise your eyes slowly. Caravaggio painted it for this room, to be seen like this, by whoever comes in." Then he opened the door.

They did as he said. The floor, dark stone. The walls, bare. And then, raising their eyes, the painting. It filled the whole far wall, five metres of darkness, with the figures at the bottom, small, as if in the corner of a courtyard. A prison. An arched doorway. The saint on the ground, already struck. The executioner bent over him, the knife behind his back. An old woman covering her face with her hands. A girl with a golden platter, ready to receive the head. And two prisoners watching the scene from a barred window, unable to do anything.

Nobody spoke for five minutes. Matei, having already seen hundreds of Caravaggios in books, thought he knew what to expect. He was wrong. Giulia, on the other hand, thought of nothing. She looked. Then Camilleri switched on a small lamp and pointed it downwards, towards the blood flowing from the saint's neck. In the red, written in the same colour, were some letters: "f. Michelang.o". "The only signature of his life," said Camilleri softly. "And he wrote it in blood. Some think it was a confession. He himself had killed a man in Rome two years earlier."

It was at that moment, looking closely at those red letters, that Giulia saw the cracks. They were tiny, thin as hairs, and ran around the signature and along the executioner's arm. Other restorers before her had already noticed them. But seeing them with her own eyes, a few centimetres away, Giulia understood what they meant: the painting, after more than four hundred years, was asking for help. Without saying anything, she took Matei's hand and squeezed it. Matei understood. There was no more need for hypotheses.

Once the visit was over, Camilleri took them to see the apartment. It was on the third floor of an old house on a street running down to the harbour, with a green gallarija looking right out over the sea. Inside there were two bedrooms, a small kitchen with blue tiles and a little roof terrace from which you could see the whole city. Viola, as soon as she was inside, ran to the gallarija, climbed onto the little sofa beneath it and stayed glued to the windows, watching the boats. Then she turned to her parents and said, with a certain authority: "Casa."

They spent Saturday walking. They visited the Grand Master's Palace, with the knights' suits of armour lined up like metal soldiers. They ate pastizzi, little parcels of puff pastry filled with ricotta, sitting on a low wall in front of the harbour. They took a ferry across the bay, and Viola, instead of being frightened like Grandma Graziella in the boat at Sorrento, laughed the whole time, trying to touch the spray with her hands. In the evening, all three of them being exhausted, they had dinner on the terrace of the apartment, which Camilleri had left them for the weekend, "to try it out".

Before dinner, though, Camilleri had taken them to see the nursery, just round the corner, in an old convent with a courtyard full of orange trees. There were three nuns, all Sicilian, all over seventy, speaking an Italian full of long vowels. The oldest, Sister Agata, took Viola by the hand without asking permission and led her off to see the hens in the courtyard. Viola, who was usually very shy with strangers, followed her without looking back. Coming back ten minutes later with an egg in her hand, she handed it to Giulia with the air of someone who has just closed an important deal. "Agata," said Giulia, looking at the nun. "Like Totò's mother." Matei laughed. "There you go," he said. "Now we can't say no. It's a sign."

On Saturday evening Camilleri invited them to dinner at his house in Sliema, on the other side of the bay. His wife Marija had made rabbit stew, the national dish, and a date cake. While eating, Giulia discovered that Maltese was a very strange language, with Arabic grammar and half its words Italian. "Grazzi" meant thank you, "skola" meant school, and "bonġu" meant good morning. "Having heard Italian for centuries, the Maltese took a piece of it," explained Marija, pouring the wine. "Just as you, after all, will take a piece of Malta. You'll see. Anyone who comes here for six months comes back for the rest of their life." At the end of dinner Viola said goodbye to everyone with a perfect "grazzi", and Marija gave her a little painted wooden boat.

It was there, on the terrace, with the harbour lights below them and Viola asleep on a sun lounger with her bunny, that Giulia and Matei really talked for the first time. No longer about hypotheses, but about concrete things. Matei could work with Giulia on the painting, as her assistant, because Camilleri had said two restorers were needed. Viola would go to an Italian nursery that existed in Valletta just round the corner, run by Sicilian nuns. And every four weeks, the flight being only an hour and a half, they could go back to Florence for a weekend.

"There are still a thousand things that could go wrong," said Giulia, looking at the sea. "I know," replied Matei. "But thinking about it carefully, there are a thousand even if we stay." They sat in silence for a long time, listening to the bells of a distant church. Then Matei took out his phone. "Shall we call Florence?" he asked. Giulia looked at the time: it was ten in the evening. "At this hour Grandma is closing the trattoria," she said. "Let's call anyway. Just to hear her shout for joy, I'd wake her even at three in the morning."

Graziella answered on the first ring, a sign that she had been waiting. Matei put it on speaker. "Well?" she asked, without even saying hello. Giulia took a deep breath. "Grandma, we've seen the painting. We've seen the house. We've seen the city." Pause. "And Viola said 'home'." On the other end of the phone there was a long silence. Then a voice that didn't sound like Graziella's, but like that of a twelve-year-old girl in the mud of 1966: "Then go. But I'll bring you the ribollita myself, in March. And this time I'll hide the jar better."

On Sunday morning, before leaving, Giulia went back alone to the Co-Cathedral. She went into the oratory, sat on the wooden bench in front of the painting and stayed there half an hour, doing nothing, as Aldo used to do on Saturdays in Bellini's workshop. Then she took a small notebook from her bag and wrote, without thinking too much, the first page of her restoration diary, as Bellini had taught her and as Ernesto had done in 1966: the date, the place, the name of the work. And underneath, a single sentence.

"Having seen the signature, I have no more doubts." She read it again, crossed it out and rewrote it differently: "After seeing the signature, I understood I couldn't say no." Then she crossed that out too and wrote the sentence that stayed for ever on the first page of the diary: "There are paintings you look at, and paintings that look at you. This one looked at me. We'll be back in March." She closed the notebook, greeted the saint with a little nod, as you greet a patient, and went out into the morning light, where Matei and Viola were waiting for her, eating a pastizzo.

The return flight left at four in the afternoon. Having tired herself out running on the bastions all morning, Viola fell asleep again before take-off. Giulia watched from the window as the island grew smaller and smaller, golden in the afternoon sun, until it disappeared beneath the clouds. Matei, beside her, was writing something on his phone. "What are you doing?" she asked. "I'm writing to Camilleri," he replied. "That he can send the contract on Monday. And that in March three of us will arrive. Plus a jar of ribollita, if it gets through security."

Arriving in Florence late at night, they found Bellini sitting in the trattoria at his usual table, pretending to read the paper. He had come "by chance", he said, even though the cardiologist had forbidden him to go out after nine. He listened to the account of the weekend without interrupting, nodding now and then. Then, when Giulia had finished, he took the old yellowed ticket from his wallet, "Catania – Valletta, 14 March 1992", and put it in her hand. "You keep it," he said. "It's no longer valid, of course. But having kept it for more than thirty years without using it, I think the time has come for someone to make that journey in my place." Giulia looked at it, then slipped it carefully into the first page of her restoration diary, next to the sentence about the painting that looks at you.
